bp: A library search box is only as useful as the catalog behind it. In many libraries, especially older or smaller ones, a book may be recorded mainly by its title, with no subject labels, summary, topic tags, or expert notes. That leaves the reader trying to guess the exact words the catalog happens to contain. Smart Book Seeker serves the everyday situation where someone knows a need but not the right title: a student looking for a Chinese-language book about a historical period, a reader trying to enter a new subject, or a patron who can describe an interest but cannot judge which candidate books truly fit it. The paper treats search as a conversation plus selection problem, not just a lookup. Its system tries to recover missing catalog knowledge by using coordinated agents that clarify the user need, search with keywords, and then discuss whether the returned books actually satisfy that need.
wh: The hard part is that the catalog has too little surface evidence. If each book has only a title, then the usual search signal is thin: the system can match words in the query to words in the title, but it cannot read a subject heading or abstract to learn what the book is about. This creates three connected failures named in the abstract. First, users may not know how to phrase the request, because they do not know the collection's wording. Second, vocabulary mismatch hides relevant books: a useful book can be missed if its title uses different words from the user's query. Third, even when candidates appear, many users lack enough domain knowledge to tell which titles really answer the need. The system therefore has to solve not only retrieval, meaning finding candidates, but also requirement clarification and result judgment under missing metadata.
naive: A smart beginner would build a keyword search over titles. The user types several words, the system returns titles containing those words, and perhaps the top results are sorted by how many words match. This is attractive because it is simple, fast, and fits the available catalog field. It fails because title words are a narrow doorway into a book. A title may be poetic, abbreviated, translated, or focused on a subtopic the user does not know to name. The beginner might then ask users to try more queries, but that shifts the hardest work onto the least prepared person. If the user cannot formulate expert vocabulary or evaluate ambiguous titles, repeated keyword search just repeats the same mismatch.
ap: The paper's core move is to split library search into three roles that cooperate. The User-Needs Agent talks with the searcher to make an unclear request more precise. The Librarian Agent turns that clarified need into keyword searches and retrieves candidate books from the sparse catalog. The User Agent then acts as a knowledgeable stand-in for the user, discussing the candidates with the Librarian Agent and selecting the best results. The important change is the third role. Traditional search assumes the user can inspect the returned list and decide what is relevant. Smart Book Seeker notices that this assumption is often false when the user lacks domain knowledge. It therefore adds a domain-knowledge-equipped proxy whose job is to judge fit, not merely to produce more query words. The agents together replace a one-shot title match with an interactive cycle of clarification, retrieval, and evaluation.
mech: The mechanism begins with an underspecified book need, not with a perfect query. The User-Needs Agent first asks or infers clarifying information through dialogue, turning a vague request into a more search-ready description. That description is passed to the Librarian Agent. Because the library has sparse metadata, the Librarian Agent still works through keyword retrieval: it must choose search terms that can be matched against available catalog text, mainly titles. It executes those searches and returns candidate books rather than claiming the first hit is enough. The User Agent then enters as a proxy reader with domain knowledge. It examines the candidate titles in light of the clarified need and discusses them with the Librarian Agent over multiple turns. In that discussion, candidates can be questioned, compared, and narrowed. The abstract frames this collaboration as the key way the system compensates for users who cannot judge results themselves. The final output is a selected top set of books. The reported evaluation uses a 20,000-book Chinese collection and measures whether the right book appears in the top results and how many of the top five are useful.
math: The main mathematical ideas are scoring, ranking, and decision under missing information. Scoring means giving each candidate book some evidence of fit: do the title words line up with the clarified need, and does the agent discussion suggest the candidate belongs to the user's topic? Ranking means putting a small number of candidates in front of the user, where early mistakes matter more because the top five results are what the paper reports. The multi-agent part adds a search process over possible interpretations of the user's need. At each turn, the system has partial evidence: the user's words, clarifications from dialogue, title matches from the catalog, and judgments made by the domain-aware proxy. It must choose whether a candidate is close enough, whether another query should be tried, and which results deserve selection. This is not magic knowledge filling the catalog; it is structured comparison when direct metadata is absent. The central tradeoff is recall versus precision: broaden the query to avoid missing relevant books, but narrow the final set so users are not handed many wrong titles. Dialogue also trades cost for certainty, spending extra interaction to reduce ambiguity.
dots: This paper sits at the crossing of information retrieval and agent tool use. In the retrieval family, it shares the old problem of choosing a few useful items from a large collection when the user's words and the collection's words do not match. It is close to query clarification and conversational search because it treats the user's first request as a starting point, not a complete specification. In the agent family, it treats language-model-like agents as workers around a search tool: one agent elicits intent, one runs retrieval, and one judges results. That resembles shopping and tool-selection systems in the repo's current family data, where an agent must turn a messy preference into search, comparison, and action. The distinctive surface here is the library setting: the scarce resource is not only compute or attention, but catalog metadata. The system is trying to reconstruct enough context around title-only records to make search usable.
ww: The approach should work better than plain keyword retrieval because it attacks the failure chain at more than one point. Clarification improves the input before search begins: if the user says something broad or ambiguous, the system can collect additional constraints instead of immediately matching weak words. The Librarian Agent keeps the practical strength of keyword search, which is important because the catalog may not contain richer fields to search. The User Agent then repairs the output side by adding judgment. A title-only hit list can contain books that share a word but not the intended topic, or books that look irrelevant to a beginner but are actually close. A domain-aware proxy can compare candidates against the clarified need and ask the retrieval agent for alternatives across several turns. This division of labor matters because each role handles a different uncertainty: what the user means, what the catalog can return, and which returned books are truly useful. The reported top-five gains fit that explanation: better intent plus better selection should raise both hit rate and precision.
po: The payoff is a library search system for collections that cannot rely on rich catalog records. On a 20,000-book Chinese collection, the abstract reports an 87 percent hit rate and 57 percent precision among the top five results. It says these are relative improvements of 28 percent and 90 percent over traditional keyword retrieval. In practical terms, the system buys two abilities: it helps users express a need when they do not know the right catalog vocabulary, and it reduces the burden of judging sparse, ambiguous title matches. That makes title-only catalogs more searchable without requiring every book to be manually enriched first.
limits: The claims depend on the agents having enough domain knowledge to judge candidate books from sparse evidence. If a title is misleading, too generic, or missing essential context, even a knowledgeable proxy may overconfidently choose the wrong item. The abstract does not show how the agents obtain or verify their domain knowledge, how much dialogue users tolerate, or whether the method works beyond the tested Chinese collection. Keyword retrieval remains a bottleneck: if the right book never appears among candidates, later discussion cannot select it. The reported metrics are strong, but they do not prove reliability for every subject area, language, catalog quality level, or real patron need.
